institutions.name: University of Vienna
institutions.summary: Founded by Duke Rudolf IV of Austria in 1365, the oldest university in today's German-speaking world. It became the intellectual centre of the Habsburg lands, with a strong mathematical-astronomical school in the 15th century and the 'Vienna medical schools' of the 18th and 19th centuries.
institutions.notes: Founding charter of Rudolf IV and papal bull of Urban V, both 1365; the theology faculty was only granted in 1384.

institutions.name: University of Heidelberg
institutions.summary: Founded by Elector Palatine Rupert I in 1386 after the Great Schism drove German masters from Paris, it is the oldest university in present-day Germany. It became a centre of Reformed theology in the 16th century and, after refoundation by Baden in 1803, a leading 19th-century research university.
institutions.notes: Papal bull of Urban VI dated 1385; teaching began in October 1386.

institutions.name: Dominican Studium Generale of Cologne
alt: Studium generale of the Dominicans in Cologne
institutions.summary: The first Dominican studium generale in Germany, established by the order's general chapter and led by Albertus Magnus. Its theological teaching made Cologne a scholastic centre long before the city had a university.
institutions.notes: End date reflects the incorporation of the mendicant studia into the theology faculty of the new university in 1388; the Dominican house itself continued.

institutions.name: University of Cologne (old)
institutions.summary: The first university in Germany founded by a city council rather than a prince, chartered by Urban VI in 1388. It remained a bastion of Thomist scholasticism and Catholic orthodoxy (the 'Dunkelmänner' of the Reuchlin affair) until the French closed it.
institutions.notes: The present University of Cologne (1919) is a new foundation outside this dataset's scope.

institutions.name: University of Erfurt (old)
institutions.summary: Chartered at the request of the city council, Erfurt was one of the largest German universities of the 15th century and a centre of humanism. Luther studied here before entering the Augustinian friary.
institutions.notes: Bull of Avignon pope Clement VII 1379; renewed by Urban VI 1389; teaching opened 1392. Some count 1392 as the start. The present University of Erfurt (1994) is outside scope.

institutions.name: University of Würzburg
institutions.summary: First founded by Prince-Bishop Johann von Egloffstein in 1402, the university soon collapsed and was refounded in 1582 by Prince-Bishop Julius Echter as a Counter-Reformation university. In the 19th century it became a leading centre of medicine and physics; Röntgen discovered X-rays here in 1895.
institutions.notes: The first foundation (1402, papal privilege of Boniface IX) faded after the murder of chancellor Johann Zantfurt in 1413; continuity with 1582 is institutional tradition rather than unbroken teaching.

institutions.name: University of Leipzig
institutions.summary: Founded in 1409 by German masters and students who left Prague after the Decree of Kutná Hora, with the support of the Wettin margraves. It became one of the largest German universities and a centre of the book trade, philology and, in the 19th century, experimental psychology.

institutions.name: University of Rostock
institutions.summary: The oldest university of the Baltic region, founded jointly by the dukes of Mecklenburg and the city of Rostock. It drew students from all of Scandinavia and the Hanseatic world and became a centre of Lutheran orthodoxy under David Chytraeus.
institutions.notes: Joint foundation by the dukes and the town council; papal bull of Martin V (1419). Exiles 1437–43 (interdict over the town) and 1487–88 (Domfehde).

institutions.name: University of Greifswald
institutions.summary: Founded in 1456 on the initiative of burgomaster Heinrich Rubenow with Duke Wartislaw IX of Pomerania. From 1648 to 1815 it was a Swedish university, the oldest in the Swedish realm after Uppsala.
institutions.notes: Papal bull of Callixtus III (1456) and imperial privilege of Frederick III.

institutions.name: University of Freiburg
institutions.summary: Founded by Archduke Albert VI of Austria in Habsburg Further Austria, it remained a Catholic university with Jesuit teaching from 1620. It passed to Baden in 1805 and in 1900 was the first German university to matriculate women.
institutions.notes: Papal bull of Callixtus III 1455; opened 1457. Temporarily at Konstanz during French occupation of Freiburg (1686–98).

institutions.name: Ludwig Maximilian University (Ingolstadt–Landshut–Munich)
institutions.summary: Founded at Ingolstadt by Duke Ludwig IX of Bavaria-Landshut, it became the leading Catholic university of Germany and a Jesuit stronghold of the Counter-Reformation. It moved to Landshut in 1800 and to Munich in 1826.
institutions.notes: Papal bull of Pius II 1459; opened 26 June 1472.

institutions.name: University of Trier (old)
institutions.summary: Chartered by Nicholas V in 1454 at the request of the archbishop, but opened only in 1473 after the city bought the privilege. It became a Jesuit-dominated institution from 1561 and was closed by the French.
institutions.notes: The bull dates from 1454 (Nicholas V) but the city acquired it from the archbishop in 1473 and opened the university that year. Present University of Trier (1970) outside scope.

institutions.name: University of Mainz (old)
institutions.summary: Founded by Archbishop-Elector Diether von Isenburg, the university of the Empire's arch-chancellor was Jesuit-dominated from 1561 and reformed in the Catholic Enlightenment under Elector Erthal. It was closed under French occupation.
institutions.notes: Bull of Sixtus IV 1476; opened 1477. Remnants (medicine/law schools) continued until 1823. Present Johannes Gutenberg University (1946) outside scope.

institutions.name: University of Tübingen
institutions.summary: Founded by Count Eberhard im Bart of Württemberg, it became the intellectual centre of Lutheran Württemberg after 1534. Its Protestant seminary, the Tübinger Stift, trained Kepler, Hegel, Hölderlin and Schelling.
institutions.notes: Bull of Sixtus IV 1476; opened October 1477.

institutions.name: University of Wittenberg
institutions.summary: Founded by Elector Frederick the Wise of Saxony, Wittenberg became the cradle of the Reformation: Luther posted the Ninety-five Theses here in 1517 and Melanchthon shaped Protestant education from its lecture halls. It was merged with Halle in 1817.
institutions.notes: Imperial privilege of Maximilian I (1502); papal confirmation 1507. Merged into u-halle-wittenberg in 1817.

institutions.name: University of Frankfurt (Oder)
institutions.summary: The first university of Brandenburg, founded by Elector Joachim I and his brother. It became Lutheran in 1539 and, after the Hohenzollerns converted, a Reformed-influenced institution; it was merged into Breslau in 1811.
institutions.notes: Papal bull of Julius II (1506) and imperial privilege; opened 26 April 1506. Present European University Viadrina (1991) outside scope.

institutions.name: University of Marburg
institutions.summary: Founded by Landgrave Philip I of Hesse as the first Protestant university, endowed with dissolved monastic property. It turned Reformed in 1605 and was disrupted by the Hessian succession conflict before being restored in 1653.
institutions.notes: Imperial privilege only in 1541. The Hesse-Darmstadt Lutheran university of Giessen occupied Marburg 1625–1650 while Reformed Hesse-Kassel taught at Kassel (u-kassel).

institutions.name: University of Kassel (Reformed, 1633–1653)
institutions.summary: The Reformed state university of Hesse-Kassel, created after Marburg passed to Lutheran Hesse-Darmstadt. It carried the Calvinist Marburg tradition until reunited with Marburg in 1653.
institutions.notes: Grew out of the Collegium Mauritianum; Reformed Marburg teaching was continued at Kassel from 1625 and given university form in 1633. Unrelated to the modern University of Kassel (1971).

institutions.name: University of Königsberg
institutions.summary: Founded by Duke Albert of Prussia as a Lutheran university for the duchy and the Baltic, it is famous above all for Immanuel Kant. In the 19th century it was a leading centre of mathematics and physics.
institutions.notes: Polish royal privilege 1560 (Prussia was a Polish fief). Ceased in 1945, outside scope.

institutions.name: University of Jena
institutions.summary: Founded by the Ernestine Saxon dukes after they lost Wittenberg in 1547, Jena was first a stronghold of Gnesio-Lutheranism. Around 1790–1806 it was the centre of German Idealism and early Romanticism, with Reinhold, Fichte, Schelling, Hegel and Schiller teaching.
institutions.notes: Hohe Schule (Collegium Jenense) opened 1548; imperial privilege of Ferdinand I 1557; inaugurated as university 2 February 1558.

institutions.name: University of Dillingen
institutions.summary: Founded by Cardinal Otto Truchsess von Waldburg, Prince-Bishop of Augsburg, as a Catholic reform university, and run by the Jesuits from 1564. Reduced to a lyceum by Bavaria after secularization.
institutions.notes: College of St Jerome 1549; papal bull 1551; imperial privilege 1553. Dissolution as university 1803/04.

institutions.name: University of Helmstedt
institutions.summary: Founded by Duke Julius of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, Helmstedt was for a time one of the largest Protestant universities and home of Georg Calixtus's irenic theology. It was dissolved by the Kingdom of Westphalia.
institutions.notes: Imperial privilege of Maximilian II 1575; opened 15 October 1576.

institutions.name: University of Altdorf
institutions.summary: The university of the Imperial City of Nuremberg: a Gymnasium moved to Altdorf in 1575, raised to an academy in 1578 and to a full university in 1622. Known for law, medicine and natural science; Leibniz took his doctorate here.
institutions.notes: Academy 1578 (imperial privilege of Rudolf II); university privileges 1622 (Ferdinand II). Closed 1809 after Nuremberg passed to Bavaria.

institutions.name: Hohe Schule Herborn
institutions.summary: Reformed Hohe Schule founded by Count John VI of Nassau-Dillenburg, never granted university privileges but of European importance for Calvinist theology, political theory (Althusius) and encyclopedism (Alsted, Comenius).
institutions.notes: Became a theological seminary of Nassau in 1817.

institutions.name: University of Graz
institutions.summary: Founded by Archduke Charles II of Inner Austria as a Jesuit university of the Counter-Reformation. Downgraded to a lyceum by Joseph II, it was restored by Francis I in 1827 and became a notable centre of physics (Boltzmann).
institutions.notes: Papal confirmation 1586.

institutions.name: Protestant Collegiate School of Graz
institutions.summary: Protestant school of the Styrian estates teaching at upper-gymnasium/academic level. Kepler taught mathematics here until the Counter-Reformation closed it.
institutions.notes: Founded by the Protestant Estates of Styria.

institutions.name: University of Paderborn (old)
institutions.summary: Jesuit university founded by Prince-Bishop Dietrich von Fürstenberg, with faculties of philosophy and theology. It survived the Jesuit suppression but lost university status under Prussia.
institutions.notes: Papal and imperial privileges 1615/16. Successor institution: philosophical-theological academy (now Theologische Fakultät Paderborn). End year uncertain (1818/19).

institutions.name: University of Giessen
institutions.summary: Founded by Landgrave Louis V of Hesse-Darmstadt as a Lutheran answer to Calvinist Marburg. Liebig's laboratory made it the world centre of chemical education in the mid-19th century.
institutions.notes: Imperial privilege of Rudolf II, 19 May 1607. Located at Marburg 1625–1650.

institutions.name: University of Rinteln
institutions.summary: Small Lutheran university of the County of Schaumburg, founded by Count Ernst of Holstein-Schaumburg. It passed to Hesse-Kassel and was dissolved by the Kingdom of Westphalia.
institutions.notes: Gymnasium illustre at Stadthagen 1610; moved to Rinteln and given university privileges (Ferdinand II) 1621.

institutions.name: Strasbourg Gymnasium and Academy
institutions.summary: Johannes Sturm's Protestant gymnasium, founded by the city council, became the model for humanist secondary schools across Europe. Raised to an academy by imperial privilege in 1566, it became the University of Strasbourg in 1621.

institutions.name: University of Strasbourg
institutions.summary: Raised from Sturm's academy to a Lutheran university in 1621, it remained German-speaking and Protestant under French rule after 1681. Abolished in the Revolution, it was replaced by Napoleonic faculties and, after 1872, by the German Kaiser-Wilhelms-Universität, a showcase research university.
institutions.notes: Modelled as one record across three phases (Lutheran university 1621–1793; French faculties 1808–1870; Kaiser-Wilhelms-Universität 1872). The Catholic episcopal university (u-molsheim) was separate.

institutions.name: Episcopal University of Molsheim/Strasbourg
institutions.summary: Jesuit university of the bishops of Strasbourg, created as a Catholic counterweight to Lutheran Strasbourg. After the French annexation it moved into Strasbourg as the episcopal university.
institutions.notes: Jesuit college 1580; papal bull 1617, inaugurated 1618; sources also give 1611 and 1621 for university status. Jesuits replaced by secular clergy 1765.

institutions.name: Benedictine University of Salzburg
institutions.summary: Founded by Prince-Archbishop Paris Lodron and run by a confederation of south German and Austrian Benedictine abbeys, a rare non-Jesuit Catholic university. Dissolved under Bavarian rule.
institutions.notes: Gymnasium 1617; university 1622 (imperial privilege 1620, papal 1625). Reduced to a lyceum 1810; refounded 1962 (outside scope).

institutions.name: University of Osnabrück (Jesuit, 1632–33)
institutions.summary: Short-lived Jesuit university founded by Prince-Bishop Franz Wilhelm von Wartenberg during the Catholic restoration in the Thirty Years' War; it ended when Swedish forces captured the city.
institutions.notes: Papal bull 1631; opened 1632. Modern University of Osnabrück (1974) outside scope.

institutions.name: University of Duisburg (old)
institutions.summary: Reformed university founded by Elector Frederick William of Brandenburg for the Duchy of Cleves; small throughout its existence, it was closed by Prussia in favour of Bonn.
institutions.notes: Imperial privilege 1566 obtained earlier but unused; opened 1655.

institutions.name: University of Kiel
institutions.summary: Founded by Duke Christian Albert of Holstein-Gottorp, it became the university of the Danish-ruled duchies after 1773 and of Prussia after 1867.
institutions.notes: Imperial privilege of Leopold I 1665.

institutions.name: University of Innsbruck
institutions.summary: Founded by Emperor Leopold I, financed by a salt tax, on the basis of the Jesuit gymnasium. Twice reduced to a lyceum (1782, 1810) and restored, it became the university of Tyrol.
institutions.notes: Jesuit gymnasium since 1562.

institutions.name: University of Halle
institutions.summary: Founded by Elector Frederick III of Brandenburg, Halle was the first 'modern' university of the Enlightenment, combining Pietism (Francke) with rationalist philosophy (Thomasius, Wolff) and teaching in German. It was merged with Wittenberg in 1817.
institutions.notes: Imperial privilege 1693; inaugurated 1 July 1694.

institutions.name: University of Halle-Wittenberg
institutions.summary: Created by the Prussian state in 1817 by uniting the universities of Halle and Wittenberg, seated at Halle. It became a major Protestant theology faculty and, later, a centre of mathematics (Cantor).

institutions.name: University of Breslau
institutions.summary: Founded as the Jesuit Leopoldina by Emperor Leopold I, with philosophy and theology faculties. In 1811 Prussia merged it with the Viadrina of Frankfurt (Oder) to form a full, bi-confessional university.
institutions.notes: Leopoldina 1702 held imperial university privileges (Catholic, two faculties); 1811 refounded as Universität zu Breslau.

institutions.name: University of Göttingen
institutions.summary: Founded by George II, Elector of Hanover and King of Great Britain, under Gerlach Adolph von Münchhausen as an Enlightenment university without theological censorship over other faculties. It became the leading research university of the 18th century and the centre of mathematics in the 19th.
institutions.notes: Lectures began 1734; formal inauguration 17 September 1737. Founding by George II as Elector (princely).

institutions.name: University of Erlangen
institutions.summary: Founded by Margrave Frederick of Brandenburg-Bayreuth as a Lutheran university; it passed to Bavaria in 1810 and absorbed Altdorf.
institutions.notes: Founded in Bayreuth in 1742 and moved to Erlangen, opening there on 4 November 1743. Imperial privilege 1743.

institutions.name: University of Bützow
institutions.summary: Pietist university founded by Duke Frederick of Mecklenburg-Schwerin after his conflict with the Rostock city council and orthodox Lutheran faculty. It was reunited with Rostock in 1789.

institutions.name: University of Bamberg (old)
institutions.summary: Jesuit Academia Ottoniana founded by Prince-Bishop Melchior Otto Voit von Salzburg, raised to a full university after the Jesuit suppression. Dissolved by Bavaria after secularization.
institutions.notes: Academy 1647 (imperial privileges 1648); law and medicine added 1735–73; 'university' from 1773. Reduced to a lyceum 1803.

institutions.name: University of Fulda
institutions.summary: Small Catholic university founded by Prince-Abbot Adolf von Dalberg on the basis of the Jesuit and Benedictine schools. It closed after secularization.
institutions.notes: Imperial and papal privileges 1732–33; opened 1734.

institutions.name: University of Münster
institutions.summary: Catholic Enlightenment university founded by Franz von Fürstenberg, minister of the Prince-Bishop of Münster, using funds of a dissolved convent. Reduced by Prussia to an academy in 1818, it regained full university status only in 1902.
institutions.notes: Privileges 1771 (imperial) and 1773 (papal); opened 1780.

institutions.name: Electoral University of Bonn
institutions.summary: Enlightenment university of the Electorate of Cologne, created by Elector Max Franz from the Maxische Akademie (1777) as a progressive rival to the old University of Cologne. It was closed under French occupation.
institutions.notes: Academy founded 1777; imperial university privilege 1784; inaugurated 1786.

institutions.name: University of Bonn
institutions.summary: Founded by Frederick William III as the Prussian university of the newly acquired Rhineland, with both Protestant and Catholic theology faculties. It became a leading centre of classical philology, history and chemistry.
institutions.notes: Distinct from the electoral university (u-bonn-electoral, 1786–98).

institutions.name: University of Berlin
institutions.summary: Founded by the Prussian state on Wilhelm von Humboldt's plan, uniting research and teaching under academic freedom. It became the model of the modern research university, with Fichte, Schleiermacher, Hegel and later Helmholtz and Planck.
institutions.notes: Named Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universität from 1828.

institutions.name: Hohe Karlsschule
institutions.summary: Duke Karl Eugen of Württemberg's elite academy, begun as a military orphanage at Schloss Solitude and raised to university rank by Joseph II in 1781. Known for medicine, cameralism and fine arts; closed after the duke's death.
institutions.notes: University privilege 1781; dissolved 1794.

institutions.name: Jesuit Lyceum of Linz
institutions.summary: Jesuit higher school in Linz teaching philosophy and canon law from 1669 and theology from 1672, without full university status. After 1773 it continued as a state lyceum and diocesan theological school, the ancestor of the Catholic Private University Linz.
institutions.notes: Continuity after 1773 through state lyceum/diocesan school.

institutions.name: Gymnasium Illustre of Bremen
institutions.summary: Reformed academic gymnasium of the city of Bremen, teaching theology, law and philosophy at university level and serving the Calvinist network of the Netherlands and northern Germany.
institutions.notes: Upper classes of the Latin school became the Gymnasium illustre 1610 (1584 sometimes given). Closed under French rule 1810.

institutions.name: Akademisches Gymnasium Hamburg
institutions.summary: Lutheran academic gymnasium bridging school and university in the city-state of Hamburg, with public lectures in natural sciences, theology and oriental languages. Its tradition fed into the Hamburg Colonial Institute and later the university.

institutions.name: Academic Gymnasium of Danzig
institutions.summary: Lutheran academic gymnasium of Danzig (in Royal Prussia) with professors of theology, law, medicine and natural sciences, one of the most important of its kind in the Baltic.
institutions.notes: Founded 1558 in the former Franciscan friary; academic level from c. 1580. Merged into the city gymnasium 1817.

institutions.name: Academic Gymnasium of Thorn
institutions.summary: Lutheran academic gymnasium in Toruń (Royal Prussia), a centre of Protestant learning in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.
institutions.notes: Gymnasium 1568; academic gymnasium from 1594. End of academic status approximate.

institutions.name: Gymnasium illustre of Zerbst
institutions.summary: Academic gymnasium of the princes of Anhalt, becoming Reformed with Anhalt's Calvinist turn; it served as a quasi-university for central German Calvinists.
institutions.notes: End date of academic status approximate.

institutions.name: Akademisches Gymnasium Stettin
institutions.summary: Ducal Pomeranian Pädagogium, refounded as the Gymnasium Carolinum under Swedish rule (1667), offering academic lectures in Stettin.
institutions.notes: Merged with the Marienstiftsgymnasium in 1805.

institutions.name: Casimirianum of Neustadt
institutions.summary: Reformed academy founded by Count Palatine John Casimir as a refuge for Calvinist professors expelled from Heidelberg when Elector Louis VI restored Lutheranism.
institutions.notes: Returned to Heidelberg when Calvinism was restored after 1583.

institutions.name: Gymnasium Arnoldinum
institutions.summary: Reformed Hohe Schule founded by Count Arnold IV of Bentheim-Steinfurt, with chairs in theology, law and medicine; in the 19th century it continued as a gymnasium.
institutions.notes: Academic status declined in the 18th century; it survived as a gymnasium.

institutions.name: Gymnasium academicum of Lingen
institutions.summary: Reformed academic gymnasium founded by William III of Orange (as Count of Lingen) to train clergy and officials for the county.

institutions.name: Gymnasium illustre of Hamm
institutions.summary: Reformed academic gymnasium of the County of Mark under Brandenburg, teaching theology and philosophy at university level.
institutions.notes: End of academic status approximate.

institutions.name: Gymnasium Casimirianum Coburg
institutions.summary: Lutheran academic gymnasium founded by Duke John Casimir of Saxe-Coburg with university-level lectures; continued as a gymnasium.

institutions.name: Schönaichianum of Beuthen
institutions.summary: Calvinist-leaning academic gymnasium founded by Georg von Schönaich in Silesia, a centre of late humanism destroyed in the Counter-Reformation.

institutions.name: Gymnasium illustre of Lauingen
institutions.summary: Lutheran academic gymnasium of the Palatinate-Neuburg princes, closed after Wolfgang Wilhelm's conversion to Catholicism.

institutions.name: Gymnasium of Hornbach
institutions.summary: Academic gymnasium of the Duchy of Palatinate-Zweibrücken in a former Benedictine abbey, preparing students for university.
institutions.notes: Moved to Zweibrücken in 1631.

institutions.name: Freiberg Mining Academy
institutions.summary: The oldest surviving mining academy in the world, founded by Prince Xavier of Saxony to rebuild the mining economy after the Seven Years' War. Werner's teaching made it the centre of geology; it trained Humboldt and Novalis.

institutions.name: Clausthal Mining Academy
institutions.summary: Mining school of the Harz under Hanover, raised to a Bergakademie in 1864.
institutions.notes: Mining lectures from 1775; Bergakademie 1864.

institutions.name: Berlin Mining Academy
institutions.summary: Prussian mining academy founded under Frederick II; merged into the TH Berlin only in 1916.
institutions.notes: Mining courses 1770; reorganized 1860.

institutions.name: Berlin Building Academy
institutions.summary: Prussian state school for architects and building engineers, housed from 1836 in Schinkel's landmark building. Merged into the TH Berlin in 1879.

institutions.name: Berlin Gewerbeakademie
institutions.summary: Peter Beuth's trade institute, the core of Prussian engineering education, renamed Gewerbeakademie in 1866 and merged into TH Berlin in 1879.

institutions.name: Technical University of Berlin
institutions.summary: Formed in 1879 by merging the Bauakademie and the Gewerbeakademie; moved into its new building in Charlottenburg in 1884. In 1899 Prussian THs were granted the right to award doctorates.

institutions.name: Prussian War Academy
institutions.summary: Higher staff college founded by Scharnhorst in the Prussian reform era; Clausewitz was its director while writing On War.

institutions.name: Pépinière (Friedrich-Wilhelms-Institut)
institutions.summary: Prussian military-medical academy training army surgeons; many leading 19th-century physicians and physiologists trained here.

institutions.name: Berlin Veterinary School
institutions.summary: Royal veterinary school of Prussia.

institutions.name: Hanover Veterinary School
institutions.summary: One of the oldest veterinary schools in Germany.

institutions.name: Karlsruhe Polytechnic
institutions.summary: The first polytechnic school in Germany, founded by Grand Duke Ludwig of Baden on the model of the École polytechnique. It became a Technische Hochschule in 1865; Hertz demonstrated electromagnetic waves here.

institutions.name: Munich Technical University
institutions.summary: Founded by King Ludwig II as the Polytechnische Schule; renamed TH in 1877. Linde developed refrigeration here and Diesel studied here.

institutions.name: Dresden Technical University
institutions.summary: Founded as the Saxon Technical School in 1828, it became a polytechnic in 1871 and a TH in 1890.

institutions.name: Stuttgart Technical University
institutions.summary: Founded as the Vereinigte Real- und Gewerbeschule, becoming a polytechnic in 1840 and a TH in 1890.

institutions.name: Darmstadt Technical University
institutions.summary: Hessian trade school of 1836, polytechnic from 1868 and TH from 1877; in 1882 it established the world's first chair of electrical engineering.

institutions.name: Hanover Technical University
institutions.summary: Founded by Karl Karmarsch as a higher trade school; Polytechnic 1847, TH 1879.

institutions.name: Collegium Carolinum Braunschweig
institutions.summary: Founded by Duke Charles I of Brunswick as an intermediate school between gymnasium and university with mathematics, sciences and modern languages; it became a polytechnic in 1862 and a TH in 1877. Gauss studied here.

institutions.name: Aachen Polytechnic
institutions.summary: Prussian polytechnic for the Rhenish-Westphalian industrial region, opened in 1870 and a TH from 1880.

institutions.name: Tharandt Forestry Academy
institutions.summary: Forestry school founded privately by Heinrich Cotta and taken over by Saxony as the Royal Forest Academy in 1816; a model for scientific forestry worldwide.

institutions.name: Hohenheim Agricultural Academy
institutions.summary: Agricultural institute founded by King William I of Württemberg after the 'year without a summer' famine; academy from 1847.

institutions.name: Möglin Agricultural Academy
alt: Königlich Preußische Akademie des Landbaus Möglin
institutions.summary: Albrecht Thaer's school of rational agriculture, the first agricultural academy in Germany, raised to royal academy in 1819.
institutions.notes: Closed 1861/62.

institutions.name: Eberswalde Forestry Academy
institutions.summary: Prussian forestry academy, first attached to the University of Berlin and moved to Eberswalde in 1830.

institutions.name: Vienna Polytechnic Institute
institutions.summary: Founded by Emperor Francis I under Johann Joseph Prechtl, the first polytechnic in the German-speaking lands; TH from 1872.

institutions.name: Theresianum
institutions.summary: Knightly academy founded by Maria Theresa to train young nobles for state service, with law, cameral sciences and languages at higher level; run by Jesuits until 1773.

institutions.name: Oriental Academy (Vienna)
institutions.summary: School for diplomats and interpreters for the Ottoman Empire and the East, founded by Maria Theresa.

institutions.name: Vienna Veterinary School
institutions.summary: Founded by Maria Theresa, one of the oldest veterinary schools.

institutions.name: Josephinum
institutions.summary: Military-surgical academy founded by Joseph II under Giovanni Alessandro Brambilla, famous for its wax anatomical models.
institutions.notes: Closed 1848, reopened 1854, closed for good 1874.

institutions.name: Theresian Military Academy
institutions.summary: Officer academy founded by Maria Theresa in the castle of Wiener Neustadt.

institutions.name: Mariabrunn Forestry School
institutions.summary: Austrian state forestry school, absorbed into the Hochschule für Bodenkultur in 1875.

institutions.name: Hochschule für Bodenkultur
institutions.summary: Austrian university of agriculture, which absorbed the Mariabrunn forestry school in 1875.

institutions.name: Leoben Mining Academy
institutions.summary: Styrian mining school founded at Vordernberg under Peter Tunner on the initiative of Archduke John and the Styrian estates; moved to Leoben 1849 and Bergakademie from 1861.

institutions.name: Joanneum / Graz Technical University
institutions.summary: Founded by Archduke John as a museum and teaching institute for sciences; its teaching became the TH Graz in 1872.

events.title: Foundation by Rudolf IV
events.desc: Duke Rudolf IV issued the foundation charter on 12 March 1365 and Pope Urban V confirmed it by bull, but without a faculty of theology.

events.title: Theology faculty and refoundation by Albrecht III
events.desc: Pope Urban VI granted the theology faculty and Duke Albrecht III issued new privileges, effectively refounding the university; masters arriving from Paris (Heinrich von Langenstein) shaped it.

events.title: First Ottoman siege and decline
events.desc: The Ottoman siege of 1529, plague and the Reformation caused student numbers to collapse during the mid-16th century.

events.title: Sanctio Pragmatica: Jesuit takeover
events.desc: Ferdinand II's Sanctio Pragmatica incorporated the Jesuit college into the university and handed the theology and philosophy faculties to the Jesuits.

events.title: Theresian reforms
events.desc: Under Gerard van Swieten's influence (from 1749), Maria Theresa placed the university under state direction, reformed medical teaching and curtailed Jesuit control; it became a state institution.

events.title: Suppression of the Jesuits
events.desc: The papal suppression of the Society of Jesus removed the Jesuits from the theology and philosophy faculties.

events.title: Closure after the 1848 revolution
events.desc: Students of the Academic Legion were central to the Vienna revolution; after the October rising was crushed, the university was closed and occupied by the military.

events.title: Thun-Hohenstein reform
events.desc: Minister Leo von Thun-Hohenstein introduced the Humboldtian model: freedom of teaching and learning, a full philosophy faculty and seminar-based research.

events.title: Women admitted to the philosophy faculty
events.desc: Women were admitted as regular students to the philosophical faculty; medicine followed in 1900.

events.title: Foundation by Rupert I
events.desc: Elector Rupert I opened the university in October 1386 under a 1385 bull of Urban VI; its first rector was the Paris master Marsilius of Inghen.

events.title: Lutheran Reformation
events.desc: Elector Ottheinrich introduced the Reformation and issued new statutes (1558) reorganizing the university on humanist-Protestant lines.

events.title: Heidelberg Catechism and Calvinist turn
events.desc: Under Frederick III the university became a leading Reformed centre; Zacharias Ursinus co-authored the Heidelberg Catechism (1563).

events.title: Capture by Tilly; Palatine Library taken
events.desc: Catholic League troops took Heidelberg in the Thirty Years' War; the Bibliotheca Palatina was sent to Rome as a gift to the Pope (1623) and teaching largely ceased.

events.title: French destruction of Heidelberg
events.desc: French troops burnt the town in the Nine Years' War; the university was dispersed and reopened only in 1700.

events.title: Refoundation by Baden
events.desc: After the Palatinate passed to Baden, Grand Duke Karl Friedrich reorganized and refunded the decayed university as a state institution; hence the name Ruperto Carola.

events.title: Women admitted as regular students
events.desc: Baden admitted women to full matriculation at Heidelberg in 1900, among the first German universities to do so.

events.title: Studium generale of the Dominicans
events.desc: The Dominican general chapter of 1248 established a studium generale at the Cologne priory under Albertus Magnus.

events.title: Bull of Urban VI and opening
events.desc: On petition of the city council Pope Urban VI issued the foundation bull on 21 May 1388; teaching began in January 1389.

events.title: Incorporation of the mendicant studia
events.desc: The existing studia of the Dominicans and other orders were incorporated into the new theology faculty.

events.title: Reuchlin controversy
events.desc: Cologne theologians led by Jacob van Hoogstraten condemned Reuchlin's defence of Jewish books, provoking the satirical Letters of Obscure Men (1515).

events.title: Jesuit Tricoronatum
events.desc: The Jesuits took over the Gymnasium Tricoronatum, giving them a dominant role in the arts faculty and reinforcing Counter-Reformation Catholicism.

events.title: Closed by the French
events.desc: After the French annexation of the Rhineland the university was abolished; it was replaced by an école centrale.

events.title: Bull of Clement VII
events.desc: The council obtained a foundation bull from the Avignon pope Clement VII in 1379.

events.title: Bull of Urban VI; opening 1392
events.desc: A new bull of the Roman pope Urban VI (1389) secured recognition in the Roman obedience; lectures began in 1392.

events.title: Reformation turmoil
events.desc: The 'Pfaffensturm' riots and the Reformation divided the town; enrolments collapsed and the university became bi-confessional, with Catholic theology retained.

events.title: Closed by Prussia
events.desc: After Erfurt passed to Prussia, the shrunken university was dissolved in 1816.

events.title: First foundation
events.desc: Prince-Bishop Johann I von Egloffstein founded a university under a privilege of Boniface IX.

events.title: Collapse of the first university
events.desc: After the murder of its chancellor and lack of funding, the first university ceased teaching.

events.title: Refoundation by Julius Echter
events.desc: Prince-Bishop Julius Echter von Mespelbrunn refounded the university with Jesuit teaching as an instrument of the Counter-Reformation.

events.title: Suppression of the Jesuits
events.desc: The dissolution of the Society removed the Jesuits from the theology and philosophy faculties.

events.title: Bavarian secularization
events.desc: Under Bavarian rule the university was reorganized on secular lines and opened to Protestant professors, including Schelling.

events.title: Foundation after the Prague exodus
events.desc: Margraves Frederick and William of Meissen founded the university, confirmed by a bull of Alexander V (September 1409); it opened on 2 December 1409.

events.title: Exodus of German masters from Prague
events.desc: Following the Decree of Kutná Hora, which gave the Bohemian nation three votes, several hundred German masters and students left Prague for Leipzig.

events.title: Reformation in Albertine Saxony
events.desc: Duke Henry the Pious introduced Lutheranism and the university became Protestant.

events.title: Secularized endowment and humanist reform
events.desc: Duke Maurice endowed the university with the former Dominican Paulinerkloster and other properties; Caspar Borner and Joachim Camerarius carried out a humanist reform of teaching.

events.title: Saxon liberal reform
events.desc: After unrest in 1830, new statutes reduced the medieval nations and increased state funding, preparing Leipzig's 19th-century expansion.

events.title: Foundation
events.desc: Dukes John IV and Albert V of Mecklenburg and the city council founded the university under a bull of Martin V (13 February 1419); theology was added in 1432.

events.title: Exile to Greifswald
events.desc: Because Rostock lay under papal interdict and imperial ban after civic unrest, the university moved to Greifswald.

events.title: Return to Rostock
events.desc: The university returned to Rostock once the ban was lifted; some masters stayed in Greifswald, preparing the foundation of a university there.

events.title: Exile to Lübeck (Domfehde)
events.desc: During the conflict over the cathedral chapter (Domfehde) the university withdrew temporarily to Lübeck.

events.title: Return from Lübeck
events.desc: The university returned to Rostock.

events.title: Lutheran Formula Concordiae Rostochiensis
events.desc: The Formula Concordiae between dukes and city settled the post-Reformation constitution of the now Lutheran university.

events.title: Reunion with Bützow
events.desc: The ducal university at Bützow, created in 1760 out of a conflict with Rostock, was reunited with Rostock.

events.title: Foundation
events.desc: Opened on 17 October 1456 with a bull of Callixtus III; Rubenow drew on Rostock masters who had stayed in Greifswald during the 1437–43 exile.

events.title: Reopening as a Lutheran university
events.desc: After the university had collapsed during the Reformation (c. 1527), Johannes Bugenhagen's church order allowed it to reopen as a Lutheran institution.

events.title: Swedish university
events.desc: By the Peace of Westphalia Western Pomerania passed to Sweden; Greifswald served as a Swedish university until 1815.

events.title: Passes to Prussia
events.desc: With Swedish Pomerania, the university passed to Prussia.

events.title: Foundation by Albert VI
events.desc: Archduke Albert VI issued the foundation charter in 1457, under a 1455 bull of Callixtus III; teaching began in 1460.

events.title: Jesuits take over faculties
events.desc: The arts and theology faculties were handed to the Jesuits to secure Catholic orthodoxy.

events.title: Exile to Konstanz
events.desc: With Freiburg under French control (from 1677/79), the university moved to Konstanz.

events.title: Return to Freiburg
events.desc: After the Peace of Ryswick returned Freiburg to Austria, the university came back.

events.title: Theresian state reform
events.desc: The university became a state institution; non-Catholics were admitted and cameral and natural sciences introduced.

events.title: Suppression of the Jesuits
events.desc: Jesuit control of teaching ended with the suppression of the Society.

events.title: Saved by Baden
events.desc: After Freiburg passed to Baden (1805) and closure was debated, Grand Duke Ludwig guaranteed its funding; it took the name Albert-Ludwigs-Universität.

events.title: First German university to admit women
events.desc: In February 1900 Baden allowed women full matriculation; Freiburg was the first German university to enrol women regularly.

events.title: Opening at Ingolstadt
events.desc: Duke Ludwig IX the Rich opened the university at Ingolstadt in 1472 under a 1459 bull of Pius II.

events.title: Arrival of the Jesuits
events.desc: Duke William IV called the Jesuits (incl. Peter Canisius); from 1556 they ran the Jesuit college and later dominated philosophy and theology.

events.title: Suppression of the Jesuits
events.desc: The Jesuits were removed; Enlightenment reformers (incl. Adam Weishaupt) gained influence.

events.title: Move to Landshut
events.desc: Elector Maximilian IV Joseph moved the university to Landshut, away from the war zone.

events.title: Renamed and reformed
events.desc: The university was reorganized as Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität on Enlightenment lines.

events.title: Move to Munich
events.desc: King Ludwig I moved the university to the capital Munich.

events.title: Opening of the university
events.desc: The city council, having acquired the papal privilege of 1454, opened the university on 16 March 1473.

events.title: Jesuit takeover
events.desc: Archbishop Johann von der Leyen gave the arts and theology faculties to the Jesuits.

events.title: Suppression of the Jesuits
events.desc: The Jesuits lost their faculties; the elector reformed the university on Enlightenment lines.

events.title: Closed by the French
events.desc: The French administration of the Rhineland abolished the university.

events.title: Opening
events.desc: Archbishop Diether von Isenburg opened the university in 1477 under a 1476 bull of Sixtus IV.

events.title: Jesuit takeover
events.desc: The Jesuits took over the teaching of philosophy and theology.

events.title: Erthal's Enlightenment reform
events.desc: Elector Friedrich Karl von Erthal refounded the university with secularized monastic endowments and appointed Protestant and enlightened professors.

events.title: Closure under French rule
events.desc: With Mainz in French hands, university teaching ceased; only special schools of medicine and law survived for a time.

events.title: Foundation by Eberhard im Bart
events.desc: Count Eberhard V opened the university in 1477 with a bull of Sixtus IV.

events.title: Reformation in Württemberg
events.desc: Duke Ulrich introduced the Reformation (1534) and reformed the university with the help of Ambrosius Blarer and Melanchthon's advice.

events.title: Founding of the Tübinger Stift
events.desc: Duke Ulrich established the Protestant seminary (Stift) for state-funded theology students.

events.title: Catholic theology and political sciences
events.desc: King William I added a Catholic theology faculty (transferred from Ellwangen) and a faculty of political sciences (Staatswirtschaft), the first in Germany.

events.title: Foundation by Frederick the Wise
events.desc: Opened 18 October 1502 under an imperial privilege of Maximilian I — the first German university founded without prior papal bull.

events.title: Papal confirmation
events.desc: Cardinal legate Raymond Peraudi's confirmation was followed by papal recognition by Julius II.

events.title: Ninety-five Theses
events.desc: Theology professor Martin Luther published his theses on indulgences (31 October 1517), starting the Reformation from the university.

events.title: Protestant statutes
events.desc: New statutes for the theology faculty, drafted by Melanchthon, made Wittenberg the model Lutheran university.

events.title: Purge of the Philippists
events.desc: Elector Augustus expelled 'Crypto-Calvinist' professors; Lutheran orthodoxy was enforced via the Formula of Concord (1577/80).

events.title: Siege and closure
events.desc: French occupation and the siege of Wittenberg during the Wars of Liberation halted teaching; the university never recovered and was merged with Halle in 1817.

events.title: Opening
events.desc: Elector Joachim I and Margrave Albrecht opened the university on 26 April 1506.

events.title: Lutheran Reformation
events.desc: Elector Joachim II introduced the Reformation in Brandenburg, converting the university.

events.title: Reformed professors
events.desc: After Elector John Sigismund's conversion to Calvinism (1613), Reformed theologians were appointed, making the Viadrina bi-confessional.

events.title: First Protestant university
events.desc: Landgrave Philip I founded the university on 1 July 1527 without papal approval, funded by secularized monasteries.

events.title: Marburg Colloquy
events.desc: Luther and Zwingli debated the Eucharist at Marburg castle, a defining moment for Protestant division.

events.title: Imperial privilege
events.desc: Emperor Charles V granted an imperial privilege recognizing its degrees.

events.title: Reformed turn
events.desc: Landgrave Maurice of Hesse-Kassel introduced Calvinism; Lutheran professors left, many to found Giessen (1607).

events.title: Hesse-Darmstadt occupation
events.desc: Marburg passed to Lutheran Hesse-Darmstadt; the Giessen university moved into Marburg while the Reformed tradition continued at Kassel.

events.title: Restoration and union with Kassel
events.desc: Landgrave William VI reopened Marburg as the Hesse-Kassel state university on 24 June 1653, closing the Kassel university and merging it in.

events.title: Prussian university
events.desc: After the annexation of Hesse-Kassel by Prussia, Marburg was expanded as a Prussian university.

events.title: Reformed university at Kassel
events.desc: Landgrave William V raised the Kassel academic gymnasium (Collegium Mauritianum) to university status to replace Marburg.

events.title: Foundation by Duke Albert
events.desc: Duke Albert founded the university on 17 August 1544 as a Lutheran institution.

events.title: Royal Polish privilege
events.desc: King Sigismund II Augustus of Poland, overlord of Ducal Prussia, granted a privilege recognizing its degrees.

events.title: Osiandrian controversy
events.desc: Andreas Osiander's doctrine of justification split the theology faculty and Lutheran Prussia.

events.title: Prussian reform era
events.desc: Under the Humboldtian reforms Königsberg gained new chairs and institutes (Bessel's observatory 1810–13, Jacobi and Neumann's mathematical-physical seminar 1834).

events.title: Inauguration as university
events.desc: After an imperial privilege of 1557, the Ernestine Hohe Schule of 1548 was inaugurated as a university on 2 February 1558.

events.title: Atheism dispute
events.desc: Fichte was dismissed after the Atheismusstreit, a landmark case for academic freedom; Jena's golden age ended after 1806.

events.title: Founding of the Urburschenschaft
events.desc: Students founded the first Burschenschaft in Jena (1815), which organized the Wartburg Festival (1817).

events.title: Carlsbad Decrees
events.desc: The German Confederation's Carlsbad Decrees, following Karl Sand's murder of Kotzebue, imposed government curators on universities, banned the Burschenschaften and led to dismissals across Germany.

events.title: Papal bull
events.desc: Julius III raised Cardinal Otto's College of St Jerome to a university.

events.title: Imperial privilege
events.desc: Emperor Charles V granted an imperial privilege.

events.title: Handed to the Jesuits
events.desc: Cardinal Otto gave the university to the Society of Jesus.

events.title: Suppression of the Jesuits
events.desc: Secular clergy took over after the Society was dissolved.

events.title: Reduced to a lyceum
events.desc: After Bavaria annexed the prince-bishopric of Augsburg, the university was dissolved and replaced by a lyceum.

events.title: Opening of the Academia Julia
events.desc: Duke Julius opened the university on 15 October 1576 under a 1575 imperial privilege.

events.title: Rejection of the Formula of Concord
events.desc: Duke Julius's refusal to adopt the Formula of Concord gave Helmstedt a distinctive humanist, 'Philippist' Lutheran profile that later nurtured Calixtus's syncretism.

events.title: Dissolved by Westphalia
events.desc: King Jérôme of Westphalia closed Helmstedt (and Rinteln), transferring resources to Göttingen and Halle.

events.title: Academy founded
events.desc: Nuremberg's council raised its Altdorf gymnasium to an academy with an imperial privilege granting the bachelor and master degrees.

events.title: University privileges
events.desc: Emperor Ferdinand II granted full university rights including doctoral degrees in all faculties except theology (granted 1696).

events.title: Closed by Bavaria
events.desc: After Nuremberg became Bavarian, the university was dissolved in favour of Erlangen.

events.title: Opening of the Hohe Schule
events.desc: Count John VI opened a Reformed academy in Herborn under Caspar Olevian and Johannes Piscator.

events.title: Reduced to a seminary
events.desc: The Duchy of Nassau converted the academy into a Protestant theological seminary.

events.title: Jesuit university
events.desc: Archduke Charles II founded the university on 1 January 1585 and entrusted it to the Jesuits.

events.title: Suppression of the Jesuits
events.desc: The Jesuits lost control of the university.

events.title: Reduced to a lyceum
events.desc: Joseph II reduced the university to a lyceum as part of his centralizing educational reforms.

events.title: Restoration by Francis I
events.desc: Emperor Francis I restored full university status; the name Karl-Franzens-Universität honours both founders.

events.title: Women admitted
events.desc: Women were admitted to the philosophical faculties of Austrian universities.

events.title: Founded by the Styrian estates
events.desc: The Lutheran estates of Styria founded a collegiate school as a counterweight to the Jesuit college.

events.title: Closed in the Counter-Reformation
events.desc: Archduke Ferdinand expelled the Protestant preachers and teachers and closed the school.

events.title: Foundation
events.desc: Prince-Bishop Dietrich IV von Fürstenberg founded the Academia Theodoriana under Jesuit direction on 10 September 1614.

events.title: Suppression of the Jesuits
events.desc: Ex-Jesuits and secular clergy continued teaching.

events.title: Loss of university status
events.desc: Prussia reduced the institution to a theological-philosophical school.

events.title: Foundation
events.desc: Landgrave Louis V raised the Giessen gymnasium (1605) to a university with an imperial privilege of Rudolf II, staffed by Lutherans who had left Marburg.

events.title: Move to Marburg
events.desc: When Hesse-Darmstadt obtained Marburg, the university was transferred there.

events.title: Return to Giessen
events.desc: After the Hessian settlement of 1648, the university was re-established in Giessen.

events.title: Liebig's teaching laboratory
events.desc: Justus Liebig set up a teaching laboratory for practical chemistry that became the model for research training worldwide.

events.title: Gymnasium illustre at Stadthagen
events.desc: Count Ernst founded a Gymnasium illustre at Stadthagen.

events.title: University at Rinteln
events.desc: The school moved to Rinteln and received imperial university privileges.

events.title: Dissolved by Westphalia
events.desc: King Jérôme's government closed the university.

events.title: Sturm's Gymnasium
events.desc: The city council founded the Gymnasium under Johannes Sturm, combining existing Latin schools.

events.title: Academy privilege
events.desc: Emperor Maximilian II raised the gymnasium's upper classes to an academy with the right to confer bachelor and master degrees.

events.title: University privileges
events.desc: Emperor Ferdinand II raised the academy to a full university.

events.title: French annexation
events.desc: Louis XIV annexed Strasbourg; the Lutheran university was allowed to continue alongside the Catholic episcopal university.

events.title: Abolished by the Revolution
events.desc: The National Convention abolished the university with all others in France.

events.title: Napoleonic faculties
events.desc: Faculties of letters, sciences, law, medicine and Protestant theology were established within the Imperial University.

events.title: Siege of Strasbourg
events.desc: German bombardment destroyed the city library and the Protestant seminary library with medieval manuscripts.

events.title: Kaiser-Wilhelms-Universität
events.desc: The German Empire founded a new university as a model research institution for the annexed Reichsland.

events.title: University inaugurated
events.desc: Archduke Leopold, Bishop of Strasbourg, had the Jesuit college at Molsheim raised to a university with papal (1617) privileges.

events.title: Transfer to Strasbourg
events.desc: The university faculties moved to Strasbourg as the Catholic episcopal university; a college remained at Molsheim.

events.title: Expulsion of the Jesuits
events.desc: Following the expulsion of the Jesuits from France, secular priests took over teaching.

events.title: Abolished by the Revolution
events.desc: Dissolved with all French universities.

events.title: University of the Benedictines
events.desc: Archbishop Paris Lodron opened the university, staffed by the Benedictine confederation.

events.title: Papal confirmation
events.desc: Urban VIII confirmed the university's privileges.

events.title: Dissolved by Bavaria
events.desc: Under Bavarian rule the university was reduced to a lyceum.

events.title: Opening
events.desc: Prince-Bishop Franz Wilhelm von Wartenberg opened a Jesuit university built on the Gymnasium Carolinum.

events.title: Swedish capture
events.desc: Swedish troops took Osnabrück and the university ceased.

events.title: Opening
events.desc: Elector Frederick William opened the university on 14 October 1655.

events.title: Closed in favour of Bonn
events.desc: Prussia dissolved Duisburg when it founded the Rhenish university at Bonn.

events.title: Foundation
events.desc: Duke Christian Albert opened the university on 5 October 1665.

events.title: Under the Danish crown
events.desc: With the Gottorp lands, Kiel passed to the Danish king and became the main university of Schleswig-Holstein.

events.title: Prussian university
events.desc: After the Prussian annexation of Schleswig-Holstein, Kiel was enlarged as a Prussian university.

events.title: Foundation by Leopold I
events.desc: Emperor Leopold I founded the university with revenue from the Hall salt surcharge.

events.title: Suppression of the Jesuits
events.desc: The Jesuits lost their teaching posts.

events.title: Reduced to a lyceum
events.desc: Joseph II downgraded the university to a lyceum; restored in 1792.

events.title: Reduced again under Bavaria
events.desc: Under Bavarian rule the university was again turned into a lyceum.

events.title: Restored by Francis I
events.desc: Emperor Francis I re-established the university (Leopold-Franzens-Universität).

events.title: Inauguration
events.desc: Elector Frederick III inaugurated the university on 1 July 1694, built around Thomasius's Ritterakademie.

events.title: Expulsion of Christian Wolff
events.desc: Under Pietist pressure, Frederick William I expelled Wolff 'on pain of the noose'.

events.title: Return of Wolff
events.desc: Frederick II recalled Wolff, marking the triumph of Enlightenment rationalism at Halle.

events.title: First German woman MD
events.desc: Dorothea Erxleben received a doctorate in medicine with special royal permission, the first woman in Germany to do so.

events.title: Closed by Napoleon
events.desc: After Jena-Auerstedt, Napoleon closed the university; it reopened under the Kingdom of Westphalia in 1808.

events.title: Reopened under Westphalia
events.desc: The university reopened as part of the Kingdom of Westphalia.

events.title: Closed again
events.desc: Napoleon closed Halle again during the Wars of Liberation.

events.title: Union of Halle and Wittenberg
events.desc: The Prussian government united the two universities on 12 April 1817, with the seat in Halle; Wittenberg retained a preachers' seminary.

events.title: Wittenberg absorbed
events.desc: The University of Wittenberg was merged into Halle.

events.title: Leopoldina
events.desc: Emperor Leopold I raised the Jesuit college to a university with faculties of philosophy and theology (charter of 21 October 1702).

events.title: Prussian rule
events.desc: Silesia passed to Prussia after the First Silesian War; the Jesuit university continued under Prussian sovereignty.

events.title: Suppression of the Jesuits
events.desc: Frederick II kept the ex-Jesuits teaching as a royal school institute.

events.title: Merger with Frankfurt (Oder)
events.desc: Prussia united the Leopoldina with the Viadrina, creating a full university with both Protestant and Catholic theology faculties.

events.title: Lectures begin
events.desc: Teaching started in October 1734 under the imperial privilege of 1733.

events.title: Inauguration
events.desc: The university was formally inaugurated on 17 September 1737.

events.title: The Göttingen Seven
events.desc: Seven professors, including the Grimm brothers, Dahlmann and Weber, protested King Ernst August's annulment of the Hanoverian constitution and were dismissed.

events.title: Prussian university
events.desc: After the annexation of Hanover, Göttingen became a Prussian university.

events.title: Doctorate for Sofia Kovalevskaya
events.desc: Göttingen awarded a doctorate in mathematics to Sofia Kovalevskaya (in absentia), one of the first to a woman in modern Europe.

events.title: Opening in Erlangen
events.desc: Margrave Frederick transferred the academy founded in Bayreuth (1742) to Erlangen, where the university opened on 4 November 1743.

events.title: Bavarian university
events.desc: With the principality of Bayreuth, Erlangen became a Bavarian university and took over resources of dissolved Altdorf.

events.title: Ducal university
events.desc: Duke Frederick the Pious established a university at Bützow, drawing ducal professors away from Rostock.

events.title: Academia Ottoniana
events.desc: Prince-Bishop Melchior Otto founded a Jesuit academy with philosophy and theology.

events.title: Full university after Jesuit suppression
events.desc: With the suppression of the Jesuits the academy was reorganized as a university with law and medicine.

events.title: Dissolved by Bavaria
events.desc: After secularization of the prince-bishopric the university was reduced to a lyceum.

events.title: Adolphsuniversität
events.desc: Prince-Abbot Adolf von Dalberg opened the university with Jesuit and Benedictine teachers.

events.title: Closure
events.desc: After the secularization of the prince-bishopric, the university was closed.

events.title: Opening
events.desc: Franz von Fürstenberg opened the university on 16 April 1780 for the prince-bishopric of Münster.

events.title: Reduced to an academy
events.desc: Prussia downgraded Münster to a theological-philosophical academy in favour of Bonn.

events.title: University inaugurated
events.desc: Elector Max Franz inaugurated the Maxische Akademie as a university on 20 November 1786.

events.title: Closed by the French
events.desc: The university was dissolved after the French annexation of the Rhineland.

events.title: Foundation by Frederick William III
events.desc: The King of Prussia founded the university on 18 October 1818, replacing Duisburg and Cologne in the Rhine Province.

events.title: Arndt suspended
events.desc: Under the Carlsbad Decrees Ernst Moritz Arndt was suspended from teaching; he was reinstated in 1840.

events.title: Humboldtian foundation
events.desc: Opened in October 1810 in Prince Henry's palace, following Humboldt's plan for the unity of research and teaching (Lehr- und Lernfreiheit).

events.title: De Wette dismissed
events.desc: Under the reaction culminating in the Carlsbad Decrees, theologian W. M. L. de Wette was dismissed.

events.title: Women as guest auditors
events.desc: Prussia allowed women to attend lectures as guest auditors (full matriculation only in 1908).

events.title: Military orphanage at Solitude
events.desc: Duke Karl Eugen founded a military orphanage at Schloss Solitude that became a military academy (1773).

events.title: Move to Stuttgart
events.desc: The academy moved into Stuttgart.

events.title: University status
events.desc: Emperor Joseph II granted university privileges.

events.title: Dissolved
events.desc: Duke Ludwig Eugen closed the school after Karl Eugen's death.

events.title: Philosophy courses
events.desc: The Jesuits began courses in philosophy and canon law in the Linz Latin school.

events.title: Theology added
events.desc: Theology courses were added.

events.title: Suppression of the Jesuits
events.desc: The Austrian state took over the higher studies as a lyceum.

events.title: Gymnasium illustre
events.desc: The council elevated the upper classes of its Latin school into an academic gymnasium.

events.title: End under French rule
events.desc: The gymnasium illustre ended when Bremen was annexed to France.

events.title: Opening
events.desc: The Hamburg council founded the Akademisches Gymnasium above the Johanneum.

events.title: Dissolved
events.desc: The Akademisches Gymnasium was dissolved; its lecture system continued in the Allgemeines Vorlesungswesen.

events.title: Opening
events.desc: The city council opened the gymnasium in the former Franciscan friary.

events.title: Converted into a city gymnasium
events.desc: Under Prussian rule it lost its academic character and became an ordinary gymnasium.

events.title: Gymnasium founded
events.desc: The council of Thorn founded a Lutheran gymnasium.

events.title: Academic gymnasium
events.desc: It was raised to an academic gymnasium.

events.title: Founded by Prince Joachim Ernst
events.desc: Prince Joachim Ernst of Anhalt established the Gymnasium illustre.

events.title: Reformed confession
events.desc: The academy followed Anhalt's adoption of the Reformed confession.

events.title: Ducal Pädagogium
